items: Set Up the Visibility System: Install a wall calendar or whiteboard in a central family area like the kitchen where everyone passes by daily to ensure the schedule remains constantly visible rather than hidden on a phone.

Set Up the Visibility System: Write every commitment affecting family movement on the calendar including appointments, work schedules, social visits, and deadlines so the entire family's obligations exist in one accessible location.

Set Up the Visibility System: Assign each family member a distinct marker color on the whiteboard or create separate color-coded calendars in Google Calendar so you can quickly identify who has commitments on any given day.

Set Up the Visibility System: Mount a tablet or old phone running Google Calendar on the wall in a common area and set it to never sleep so the schedule displays continuously without requiring anyone to pull out a device.

Build the Check-First Habit: Stop answering verbal questions about the schedule and redirect every family member to consult the calendar first, repeating this response consistently until checking becomes automatic behavior.
Build the Check-First Habit: Have a direct conversation with your partner stating that you will stop reminding them about the schedule and they need to check the calendar themselves from now on.

Build the Check-First Habit: Cease all verbal schedule announcements and commit to posting every event on the calendar first before telling anyone, ensuring the calendar—not your memory—is the source of truth.

Build the Check-First Habit: Establish a morning routine where family members glance at the shared calendar before asking about the day's activities, making checking the calendar the first instinct rather than asking you.
Enforce the New Rules: Adopt the rule that if something is not written on the calendar it does not happen, rejecting all oral agreements and insisting nothing is official until it appears in writing.

Enforce the New Rules: Redirect every single request for schedule information back to the calendar without exception, even when it feels uncomfortable, to establish that checking the calendar is non-negotiable.

Enforce the New Rules: Persist through the first few weeks of discomfort when family members forget and ask you anyway, understanding that temporary friction is necessary to build lasting behavioral change.

Enforce the New Rules: Add any existing commitments that were only discussed verbally to the calendar retroactively, treating this as an opportunity to reinforce the new standard that everything goes on the calendar.
